note: Registry of every source the company-directory pipeline is allowed to read. Consumed by scripts/generate-company-directory-v2.mjs, which refuses to build from a source absent here, and rendered into docs/company-data-sources.md. `status` is the decision the pipeline acts on: `adopted` means a layer may read it today, `candidate` means licensed/terms checked but not wired up, `rejected` means a documented reason it must not be used.

sources.name: Wikidata
sources.coverage: worldwide; ~100k organisations with an official website (P856). Skewed to whatever has Wikipedia articles.
sources.company_types: every notable organisation, mixed with defunct, fictional and non-company entities
sources.domain_fields: P856 official website only. No email domain, ever.
sources.update_frequency: continuous; query service is a live SPARQL endpoint
sources.access_method: SPARQL over HTTPS (https://query.wikidata.org/sparql); bulk dumps for full copies
limitations: P856 is the official WEBSITE, not the employee email domain - it is a website signal only
notability-gated: a company needs Wikipedia sitelinks to be present, so most small and mid-size employers are missing
P856 is occasionally wrong (a successor's site, a landlord's page), which is why scripts/generate-company-directory.mjs refuses low-sitelink entities whose name and domain look unrelated
bulk queries are rate-limited and time out easily; the query service is not an SLA-backed API
sources.notes: Already the source of the committed 4,574-company seed. In v2 it stays the discovery layer, but every domain it supplies is classified `primary_website` with email confidence `unknown`.

sources.name: GLEIF LEI (Global Legal Entity Identifier) golden copy
sources.license: GLEIF LEI Data Terms of Use - free to use and redistribute, no warranty; check the current terms before shipping a product on it
sources.commercial_use: yes, under the terms page above
sources.coverage: ~2.5M legal entities that participate in financial transactions; strongest for regulated financial, listed and large private entities
sources.company_types: legal entities with an LEI: banks, funds, subsidiaries, SPVs, some public bodies
sources.domain_fields: none. LEI reference data carries names, addresses, registration identifiers and parent relationships - not websites and not email domains.
sources.access_method: free bulk download (concatenated + delta files), plus a search API
limitations: no domain data at all: every LEI entity starts with an empty domain slot
financial-participation bias: a mid-size software company may have no LEI while an empty fund does
names are legal names ('ACME TECHNOLOGIES INTERNATIONAL HOLDINGS B.V.'), which need heavy normalisation before they can be searched
the relationship field carries a parent, but it is filer-declared and sometimes stale after an acquisition
sources.notes: The strongest available open parent/subsidiary source (12.8M relationship records), and the reason the pipeline separates company entities from the domains they use. Requires a normaliser step (legal suffix stripping, case folding) before names can be matched against Wikidata labels.

sources.name: UK Companies House
sources.license: Open Government Licence v3.0 for the data on the register; the API terms add rate limits
sources.commercial_use: yes (OGL permits commercial reuse with attribution)
sources.company_types: all UK registrations: ltd, plc, LLP, dormant, dissolved
sources.domain_fields: none. The register has names, addresses, SIC codes and officers.
sources.update_frequency: continuous; free streaming API pushes changes
sources.access_method: REST API (free key) + bulk product downloads (CSV) + streaming API
sources.layer: A discovery (UK only) + C quality signals (SIC industry, active/dissolved status)
limitations: no domains: a UK discovery layer still needs a separate website-resolution step
millions of rows are dormant or dissolved; the pipeline must filter on status before it becomes a directory
contains non-company registrations (charities, LLPs, some public bodies) that a company picker should not offer
attribution and OGL conditions apply to redistributed derivatives
sources.notes: The template for every other national registry adapter: one adapter per jurisdiction, all normalised into the same entity shape.

sources.name: SEC EDGAR (US filings)
sources.license: US government work - public domain; EDGAR access requires a declared User-Agent and rate limits
sources.coverage: all US-listed registrants and many foreign private issuers
sources.company_types: listed and reporting companies (10-K/20-F filers), funds
sources.domain_fields: none directly, but filings are full-text searchable and routinely contain the issuer's email domain in exhibit letters, contact blocks and exhibits filed as documents. Excluded exhibits (e.g. material contracts) are legitimate first-party documents.
sources.access_method: EDGAR full-text search API + submissions JSON + bulk archives
limitations: listed companies only: meaningless as a discovery layer for a 500k global directory
evidence extraction needs document parsing, not a field read
rate limits are enforced (10 requests/second, declared User-Agent)
sources.notes: A first-party document that prints an address on the issuer's own domain is HIGH-quality email-domain evidence. This is the cheapest legitimate way to raise confidence above 'website domain'.

sources.name: OpenCorporates
sources.license: Open Database License (ODbL) for the open tier, with share-alike and attribution duties; bulk and commercial use require a paid agreement; several national registers inside it are NOT openly licensed
sources.commercial_use: only under a commercial licence; the free API tier forbids bulk extraction
sources.country_coverage: global but uneven; some jurisdictions are stubs
sources.company_types: registered legal entities, including many that no picker should offer
sources.access_method: REST API (key, rate-limited) + paid bulk data
limitations: ODbL share-alike on a derivative database is a licence obligation this project has not accepted
the free tier's terms prohibit the bulk extraction a 500k build needs
no domain data, so it would still need the whole website/email resolution layer on top
sources.notes: Rejected on terms, not on quality. If the directory ever needs it, the path is a paid agreement, and the licence decision belongs to whoever owns the product's legal posture - not to a generator script.

sources.name: Commercial company databases (Crunchbase, ZoomInfo, D&B, Apollo, Clearbit-style data brokers)
sources.license: proprietary subscription terms; typically forbid redistribution of the dataset and of derived domain->company mappings
sources.commercial_use: yes, under a paid subscription that usually prohibits redistribution
sources.coverage: high, including domains and (for some vendors) verified business email patterns
sources.domain_fields: website domain, and in some products 'work email domain' fields
limitations: redistribution of the dataset - which is what a seeded directory is - is normally prohibited
vendor 'work email domain' fields carry no provenance and cannot be audited
cost scales with rows, which is the opposite of what a seed wants
sources.notes: Usable only as an internal verification aid under a licence that permits it, never as committed seed data.

sources.name: Common Crawl
sources.license: the crawl is openly available; the crawled CONTENT remains the copyright of each site and re-use must respect each site's terms and robots directives
sources.commercial_use: yes for the data, subject to the crawled sites' own terms
sources.coverage: billions of pages; host-level index covers most reachable domains
sources.company_types: not a company source: a page/host source
sources.domain_fields: hostnames and page text - the raw material for extracting published email addresses and MX hostnames
sources.access_method: S3/HTTP index files and WARC/WAT/WET archives
sources.layer: D email-domain evidence (published role addresses, contact/imprint pages)
limitations: extraction targets are individual addresses; only the DOMAIN may be stored, never the address or the person
page text is untrusted: a domain mentioned in an article is not the article author's employer
large volumes: a per-company fetch is far cheaper than a crawl-wide scan for a first pass
respect robots.txt and site terms for any live fetching
sources.notes: The realistic source for step 4 of email-domain discovery: fetch a company's own /contact, /legal, /impressum, /.well-known/security.txt pages and keep only the domains of published addresses.

sources.name: Public DNS (MX, TXT/DMARC, SPF) and RDAP
sources.license: DNS resolution is public infrastructure; RDAP responses carry registry terms and are rate-limited per registry; most registrant data is redacted
sources.commercial_use: resolution yes; bulk RDAP harvesting is against several registries' terms
sources.domain_fields: MX hosts, SPF include/ip4 ranges, DMARC policy, nameservers - supporting evidence that mail infrastructure exists, and WHICH provider runs it
sources.access_method: DNS queries from the resolver of your choice; RDAP over HTTPS
limitations: MX proves that mail for the domain is hosted somewhere - it does NOT prove employees use the domain
Google/Microsoft/Mimecast MX records are shared by millions of unrelated domains, so the MX host says nothing about the company
SPF include lists leak the ESP, not the employer
parked domains and registrar parking often still answer MX
sources.notes: Recorded in the evidence model as weight 1 and never sufficient alone; see docs/company-email-domain-resolution.md.

sources.name: Certificate Transparency logs (Google CT, and the search interface at https://crt.sh)
sources.license: public log data; the search interface at https://crt.sh has its own terms for bulk use
sources.coverage: every publicly trusted TLS certificate issued since 2013
sources.domain_fields: certificate SANs - useful for discovering that `mail.company.com` or `company.net` belongs to an organisation, and for proving two domains share an operator
sources.access_method: HTTP queries against https://crt.sh, Google's CT API, or the log endpoints directly
limitations: a certificate proves control of a hostname at issue time, not employment
wildcard certificates hide hostnames; many organisations use one CDN certificate for thousands of domains
shares an operator is not the same as same legal entity (agencies, SaaS platforms, acquisitions in progress)
sources.notes: Best used to find a company's own additional hostnames, which is how a website domain is resolved down to the registrable email domain.

sources.name: ROR (Research Organization Registry)
sources.company_types: universities, institutes, hospitals with research mandates, government labs
sources.domain_fields: website domain, and often several (per-country and per-institute)
sources.access_method: free bulk JSON/CSV + REST API, no key
sources.layer: A discovery (academic employers) + B website domain
limitations: academic employers only
no email-domain field; institutional addresses still need the evidence layer

the current pipeline deliberately EXCLUDES academic TLDs (see docs/company-data-quality.md) - adopting ROR means revisiting that policy, because a university is a real employer whose staff have real institutional addresses
sources.notes: Included to make the policy question explicit rather than silent.

sources.name: Tranco list / Cisco Umbrella top-1M
sources.license: Tranco is a research list, free to use with citation; Cisco Umbrella publishes its top-1M for download under Cisco's terms
sources.commercial_use: Tranco: yes with citation; Umbrella: yes under Cisco terms
sources.layer: C ranking signal + D parked-domain detection
limitations: popularity is not company size, and a domain high in the list may be a CDN, an ISP portal or an ad network
absurdly skewed to consumer services and to English
cannot discover a company that has no website
sources.notes: Useful as one documented input to a traffic-independent ranking signal, and for spotting that a domain in the directory is actually a hosting platform.
